## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Ambaṭṭha Sutta* (DN 3) recounts an encounter in which the arrogant young brahmin student Ambaṭṭha disparages the Buddha's clan (the Sakyas), but is systematically questioned and humbled [SuttaCentral]. In defending the pedigree of the Sakyas against Ambaṭṭha's slurs, the Buddha recounts their ancestral foundation myth: the banished sons of King Okkāka (Sanskrit Ikṣvāku) retreated to the slopes of the Himalayas and cohabited (*saṃvāsa*) with their own sisters out of concern to maintain caste purity [Silk 2009]. During their debate, when Ambaṭṭha hesitates to answer a probing genealogical question, the yakkha Vajrapāṇi appears in the sky holding a blazing iron hammer (*ayokūṭa*), threatening to shatter his head into seven pieces if he does not speak the truth [Gergely; SuttaCentral]. The text also discusses the thirty-two bodily marks of a great man (*mahāpurisa*), noting that Ambaṭṭha required the Buddha to manifest supernatural powers in order to inspect the two concealed bodily marks [Kingsbury 2002; Nakamura 1999].
Scholars have observed that DN 3, together with DN 4 (*Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta*) and DN 5 (*Kūṭadanta Sutta*), forms a tightly knit stylistic and thematic cluster that presupposes the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2) and reflects a relatively developed stage of literary composition [Kingsbury 2002]. Buddhaghosa's commentary (*Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*) elaborates on the narrative, explaining the rationale behind the Sakyan sibling unions in light of caste suitability [Silk 2009].
The sutta possesses an extensive parallel tradition across Indian and non-Indian Buddhist corpora. Curated parallels include a discourse in the Chinese *Dīrghāgama* (DĀ 20), an independent early Chinese translation (T 20) datable to before 374 CE that unusually introduces vegetarian monastic precepts [Greene 2016; SuttaCentral], as well as Tibetan translations in the Kangyur (D 1 and D 6 in the Vinaya) [Levman 2014; SuttaCentral] and Sanskrit fragments (SHT sutta26, SF 43) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus computational data corroborates these alignments, identifying substantial textual overlap with the Tibetan *Vinayavastu* (D 1) and *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (D 6), the Chinese *Dīrghāgama* (T 1), and the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu* and *Śayanāsanavastu* [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali canon, the sutta shares large shared formulaic segments with DN 4, DN 5, the *Brahmāyu Sutta* (MN 91), the *Sela Sutta* (MN 92 / Snp 3.7), and the Vinaya *Khandhakas* (Kd 1, Kd 6), particularly regarding the examination of the thirty-two marks and the standard exposition of the gradual training [DharmaNexus; SuttaCentral].
